stories.title: VendingBench
stories.summary:
↳ WHAT'S NEW
VendingBench is a frontier evaluation benchmark from Andon Labs designed to test AI agents on long-horizon, economically-grounded tasks — specifically, running a simulated vending machine business across multiple decision cycles. Tested models span Anthropic's full Claude lineup from Haiku to the unreleased Mythos.

↳ THE REAL STORY
Most evals measure single-turn correctness or short reasoning chains. VendingBench forces models to manage inventory, pricing, and cash flow over extended sequences — the kind of compounding decision-making that actually breaks agents in production. If your use case involves autonomous agents running multi-step business logic (procurement workflows, dynamic pricing, resource allocation), a model's score here is more predictive than MMLU or HumanEval. The inclusion of Claude Mythos — a model not yet publicly available — also suggests Andon Labs has benchmark-partner access, meaning results may preview capability jumps before public release.
stories.considerations: The vending machine framing is concrete enough to be useful, but narrow enough to question generalization. A model that optimizes simulated restocking decisions may still fail at structurally similar but domain-shifted tasks — medical inventory, ad budget pacing, logistics. The deeper open question: does VendingBench measure genuine long-horizon planning, or does it reward models that have seen enough business-simulation data to pattern-match the scenario? Until the task construction methodology is fully public and adversarially stress-tested, treat top scores as a promising signal, not a deployment guarantee.

stories.title: Co-Existence and the End of Co-Intelligence
stories.summary:
↳ WHAT'S NEW
Ethan Mollick's latest One Useful Thing post shifts framing from 'co-intelligence' — humans and AI working together as partners — toward something he calls 'co-existence': a world where AI systems operate with enough autonomy that the collaboration metaphor starts to break down.

↳ THE REAL STORY
The practical implication is a mental model update for builders. If you've been designing workflows around human-AI teaming — where the human steers and the AI assists — Mollick is signaling that the gap between 'tool' and 'agent' is closing faster than most product assumptions account for. The post also includes a worked example of pitching a book to an AI, which functions as a concrete demo of how AI systems now handle open-ended, judgment-heavy tasks that previously required a human audience.
stories.considerations:
↳ WORTH WATCHING
The excerpt provided is thin — one teaser line — so there's a real risk of over-reading the framing shift. 'Co-existence' could be a genuine conceptual update or it could be a book-cycle rebranding. Worth reading the full post before updating your architectural assumptions. The more honest question it raises: if the collaboration metaphor is ending, what does that mean for the human oversight layer most teams have quietly assumed would always be there?

stories.title: Google Employees Internally Share Memes About How Its AI Sucks
stories.summary:
↳ WHAT'S NEW
Google employees are circulating internal memes mocking the quality of the company's own AI products, according to 404 Media. Separately, after the story published, Google's PR team quietly asked the outlet to swap out a statement — removing the line that said "it's critical that we maintain humans in the loop."

↳ THE REAL STORY
Internal dissent at this scale is a signal worth taking seriously. Engineers and PMs living inside these systems daily tend to have a more accurate read on product quality than press releases do. The meme-sharing isn't just venting — it reflects a gap between what Google ships publicly and what its own people think is ready. For developers evaluating Gemini against alternatives, this is a data point: the people closest to the model apparently share your frustrations.
stories.considerations:
↳ WORTH WATCHING
The statement edit is the more interesting detail here. Pulling "humans in the loop" language after publication isn't a typo fix — it's a policy signal. Google appears to be walking back even rhetorical commitments to human oversight, possibly to avoid creating compliance or liability anchors as automation expands. Watch whether that phrasing disappears from other official communications too.

stories.title: AI enthusiasts are in a race against time, AI skeptics are in a race against entropy
stories.summary:
↳ WHAT'S NEW
Charity Majors (Honeycomb CTO) published an essay framing the AI adoption debate as two asymmetric races: enthusiasts racing against time to ship before competitors do, skeptics racing against entropy — the slow degradation of codebases they can no longer fully understand or control.

↳ THE REAL STORY
The framing is useful because it drops the usual 'believers vs. luddites' binary. Both sides are trying to ship good software. Enthusiasts accept short-term legibility debt hoping velocity compounds into advantage before the debt comes due. Skeptics are watching AI-assisted codebases accumulate changes nobody fully reviewed, and they're betting that entropy — not a competitor — is what kills most projects. For teams making concrete decisions today about how much AI-generated code to merge without deep review, this is the actual tension on the table.
stories.considerations: The honest catch: neither race has a clear finish line, which makes both positions unfalsifiable in the short term. An enthusiast can always say 'we just need more time'; a skeptic can always point to the next incident. What's missing from most of these debates — and from the excerpt available here — is empirical data on where AI-assisted codebases actually break down versus where they hold. Until teams start publishing post-mortems that isolate AI-generated code as a variable, this stays a values argument dressed up as an engineering one.
